headline: SK Hynix ADR trades at 40% premium to local Korean shares, suggesting Korea discount persists despite KOSPI rally
reasoning: Arnad notes that SK Hynix's ADR in the US now trades at a 40% premium to the local Korean share price, indicating that a meaningful Korea discount still exists despite the KOSPI having risen from 5,000 to 9,000 and correcting back to around 6,000. He argues this gap can still close, suggesting upside for Korean equities broadly. KOSPI volatility is described as extremely high.
quote: It's very interesting that Hynix had that ADR listing two months ago or so. And that stock in the US now trades at a 40% premium to the local share. So that tells you that it's not too late to say we still have a Korea discount, right? Because the same equity in the US cost 40% more than in Korea. So there is still more to go, although KOSPI has gone from 5,000 to 9,000 and now back to 6 in a bit. So it's super volatile, but I think there is still a gap to be closed there.

headline: Consumer sector flagged as the key risk area as purchasing power erodes despite resilient spending
reasoning: Arnad identifies consumers as the weakest link in the current earnings broadening story. While consumer spending remains elevated, consumers are complaining about prices still rising, which is the flip side of companies maintaining pricing power in an above-normal inflation environment. He describes the consumer as 'a little bit so-so' and considers it the risky sector to watch.
quote: Consumers are still a little bit so-so, right? And that's with consumer spending still up there. So that's sort of the risky sector to me... companies have pricing power with this kind of just above normal inflation. And both in America and Europe and emerging markets. Yeah, and that's why consumers are complaining, because they still see prices going up. And that's, yeah, the flip side of good earnings, of course, is also the purchasing power of people that may not be as good.

headline: Jackson Hole and G20 central bank meetings in late August key watch points for Fed policy divergence and Bank of Japan rate outlook
reasoning: Arnad flags the Jackson Hole conference on August 27-28 as a key event, noting that central bankers globally are debating whether to continue following the Fed or chart independent courses. Immediately after, the G20 finance ministers and central bankers meeting in North Carolina is also significant, where Besant is expected to discuss the Bank of Japan raising interest rates with Governor Ueda. These meetings will test how much influence the US still holds over global monetary policy.
quote: Jackson Hall, beautiful Wyoming. Yeah. Yeah. So that's the big conference for all central bankers around the world. And recently, and we saw that with the Yen, there has been a bit of a debate with the central bankers and they can't seem to agree. And they're unsure whether they should still listen to the Fed or whether they should sail their own course. So we'll see whether they can agree to something on August 27 and 28. And then straight after that, they all go to North Carolina of all places to have the G20 finance ministers and central bankers meeting. And that's also the place where Besant has said that he will have a word with Weida-san from the Bank of Japan about raising interest rates there.

headline: Yen intervention via rare US-Japan joint action signals structural shift but yen carry trade remains costly
reasoning: Arnad notes that the Bank of Japan and US Treasury/Ministry of Finance conducted a joint currency intervention to underpin the yen, described as a very rare event. However, he explains that Besant appeared to act in self-interest by selling euros rather than dollars and ensuring Japanese institutions did not sell US Treasuries as payment for the intervention. The yen carry trade still carries a negative carry of approximately 2.5% per year against the dollar, making it a costly trade that needs to work quickly to be profitable.
quote: The yen has been an obvious one for years, but it's also a trade that has never really worked because you have that negative carry against you, i.e. the interest rate in Japan is one, and the interest rate in the US is three and a half... So it has to be a trade that works quite quickly. And so far that hasn't happened until suddenly then, two weeks ago, it was announced that both the Bank of Japan and the US Treasury were actually the Ministry of Finance in Japan, I should say, and the US Treasury were cooperating in underpinning the yen and going for a joint intervention, which is the rarest of things.

headline: Hyperscaler free cash flow deteriorating rapidly as heavy capex investment offsets strong earnings growth, raising return-on-capital questions
reasoning: Arnad flags that while the earnings of the largest tech companies (hyperscalers) are strong, free cash flow is diminishing quickly due to aggressive capex spending on AI infrastructure. Robeco views free cash flow as the most important yardstick for equities. A key misconception is that markets assume AI investments will generate the same return on capital as prior investments, which may not hold. As long as returns exceed the cost of capital (around 10-12%), economic value is being added, but this could still disappoint investors. The hyperscalers are also issuing very long-term bonds (50-year maturities) that compete with government bonds and are contributing to rising long-dated yields.
quote: What we're seeing is that the earnings of particularly those hyperscaler companies, the very large tech companies, are really good. But the free cash flow is diminishing quite quickly as they invest a lot in K-PEX. And that is something that's definitely on the minds of markets now. And that's particularly in the credit market now, a big issue with the issuance of lots and lots of debt paper... I think one of the misconceptions there is that people assume that or expect that these investments will have the same return on capital as the old investments. That may not be the case, but as long as that return on capital is the same or higher than the cost of capital, you're still adding economic value as we used to define it.

headline: Investment-grade credit spreads at attractive levels but bond investors risk a siren-song trap as more supply may push spreads wider
reasoning: Arnad uses the Odyssey metaphor to describe the dilemma for bond investors: hyperscaler long-dated bonds offer attractive yields well above what their credit ratings would suggest, with generous new-issue concessions. However, with tens of billions being issued regularly adding up to trillions, spreads may widen further, making it a siren song — attractive but potentially dangerous. The question for bond investors is whether to buy now or wait for supply to clear.
quote: For bond investors, it's really sort of the question, do I go for this? Or is there still more of this stuff coming out, which means that spreads may go even wider. And to me, this is interesting. It's a bit of a siren song there that you think, Oh my God, these spreads are so high. They are so attractive. We're going to make a link to the Odyssey... the bond investors are listening to this siren song and say, do I go for it and jump into the water and maybe sail my ship onto the cliff? Or am I going to tie myself to the mast and sail through this and wait for things to clear up?

headline: Robeco remains overweight equities as earnings season beats underpin the bull market despite lurking volatility
reasoning: Arnad notes that while individual stock volatility is high, broad market indices have remained resilient and earnings beats have been a key support. This quarter 85% of US companies beat estimates, up from 80% last quarter, and two-thirds to three-quarters of European and Japanese companies also beat. Free cash flow growth is a concern for hyperscalers investing heavily in capex, but the team views earnings as a strong underpinning for equities. The team's stance is still overweight equities as long as economies stay healthy and earnings growth continues to broaden beyond IT into financials and materials.
quote: So there is a lot of geopolitical tensions which are brushed aside by the markets for sure, as long as earnings are good. And as long as that's also important, economies stay healthy, right? And that's, well, so far, so good. Indeed, Europe is even better than expected. The US is slightly weaker than expected, but that's fine, because it doesn't mean that rates will be raised. So we're sort of in a positive scenario where as long as that continues, it could be good. And we need to see that broadening that has started a little bit from IT, but in financials also earnings growth is really very healthy. But consumers are still a little bit so-so, right?

headline: Fed rate hike in September seen as less likely as US economy cools, but not fully off the table
reasoning: Arnad explains that while the Fed had been contemplating a rate hike and meeting minutes confirmed this thinking, the latest economic data showing a cooling US economy — particularly in the labour market — has reduced that probability. Inflation data is benign in both the US and Europe. The US Treasury's shift to short-term debt issuance makes keeping the Fed funds rate low politically important. Arnad frames this as a positive scenario for equities as long as it continues.
quote: And the beat goes on... the benign inflation numbers also mean that the Fed is no longer seen to become active, right? For a while, we thought, okay, that it was worse, although he doesn't want to might have to raise interest rates. And the minutes also showed that the Fed is thinking about doing that. But the latest numbers, and that's why I highlight these economic surprises, are showing that the US economy is cooling, and therefore might not need a rate hike. So the hike is off the table? Not off the table, but just less likely.

headline: European economy surprising to the upside over summer, outperforming depressed expectations
reasoning: Arnad highlights a notable divergence between Europe and the US in economic surprise data, with Europe performing much better than anticipated while the US is cooling, particularly in the labour market. European earnings also showed two-thirds to three-quarters of companies beating estimates. French bond spreads are beginning to widen again, however, which warrants monitoring.
quote: What I also noted was very interesting divergence between Europe and the US in terms of economic surprises, that in Europe, actually, the economy has performed much better than people were anticipating over summer. While in the US, things are cooling down a little bit in well in the labor market in particular.

headline: Materials sector benefiting from AI ripple effect and supply scarcity, with copper in particularly hot demand
reasoning: Arnad suggests the materials sector is seeing some ripple effect from the AI boom, with copper in particularly hot demand. Supply scarcity linked to ongoing tensions in the Gulf is also contributing. This is part of the broader earnings broadening story away from pure IT, with financials and materials both showing healthy earnings growth.
quote: Yeah, there might be some of that in the material sector, for sure, with copper being in hot demand, for instance, and generally a lot of materials being scarce also because of what's going on in the Gulf. So that is a bit of a ripple effect, for sure.

headline: Strong Chinese IPO appetite signals Asian retail and institutional investors are only beginning to engage with equity markets
reasoning: Arnad highlights two major recent Chinese IPOs: CXMT, a DRAM producer that was 500 times oversubscribed in an 8.5 billion euro offering, and Unitree, a robotics company that was 8,000 times oversubscribed with the stock jumping 460% on the first day. He interprets this as evidence of significant pent-up demand for equities among Asian investors and believes this trend has much further to run.
quote: We've had two very big IPOs there. So CXMT, the DRAM producer came to the market and was heavily subscribed 500 times or something. And it wasn't a small IPO. 8.5 billion euros was issued there. And then we had Unitree, the dancing robots... the dancing robots of Unitree were even 8,000 times oversubscribed, and the stock jumped 460% on the first day. So there is definitely appetite there in Asia for equities. So there's still a lot of interest in Asia. And it feels to me like Asian investors are still only at the surface active and there's more to come there.

headline: US bond market faces rising yields driven by excessive government debt supply rather than inflation fears, raising fiscal sustainability concerns
reasoning: Arnad highlights that US Treasury yields are at new highs since the financial crisis, but TIPS markets are not signalling stress, suggesting the driver is supply rather than inflation. Governments are not cutting deficits and bond buyers are scarce. The debasement trade — moving from currencies and bonds into gold, silver, and Bitcoin — is gaining traction, suggesting loss of confidence in the US dollar as a safe haven. The US Treasury's Operation Twist (bond buybacks) is seen as counterproductive as it raises debt per bond outstanding.
quote: It seems like we can't really find buyers and people talk about ABB, anything but bonds. And you see slowly French spreads starting to widen again. Of course, there's been a lot of debates... But a lot of debates about the US Treasury market, where we're also seeing new highs in yields since the financial crisis. So that all sounds a little bit scary. But at the same time, inflation numbers are looking okay, both in Europe as well as in the US inflation is coming down. And also the tips market, the inflation adjusted markets, is not really showing signs of stress. So it's not that we're worried about inflation. We are really worried about too much supply of bonds and governments not really cutting their deficits.

headline: Software sector progressively strengthening as fears of AI displacing software revenues fade
reasoning: Arnad notes that while semiconductor stocks suffered a significant dip during intra-summer volatility linked to a leveraged fund blowup, software stocks have progressively strengthened throughout that period. He interprets this as evidence that the market's worry about AI eating into software revenues is fading, a positive signal for the sector's earnings durability.
quote: The semis had a big dip and then recovered. But software has actually progressively been strengthening throughout that period, showing that the worry about AI eating software's lunch is fading a little bit.

headline: Gold and Bitcoin strengthening on debasement trade as confidence in US dollar wanes
reasoning: Arnad notes that despite high real yields — which should theoretically suppress gold — the gold price is rising, driven by concerns about US dollar debasement. When Treasury Secretary Besant announced the bond buyback programme, both gold and Bitcoin spiked, confirming that markets are seeking alternatives to USD. Silver is also mentioned as a potential beneficiary. The debasement trade reflects concerns that the US government is issuing too much debt with no credible plan to rein it in, leaving the central bank in a bind.
quote: Recently, especially in the last weeks, when we saw some action around the dollar or sort of weakening of the dollar, the gold price actually strengthened quite a bit, suggesting that people are, again, worried about the debasement trade, as they used to call it, right, that the US government is making a fool of itself, is issuing too much debt, and nobody is reining it in. And therefore, the central bank is in a bind. And that's, yeah, there is no longer the safety of US dollars. So then you look for safety in gold. Yes, the debasement trade basically is moving money from currencies, bonds to gold, but also maybe silver this time, maybe even Bitcoin.

headline: Hyperscaler earnings season is key risk event — any signal that AI capex is peaking would cause significant market disruption
reasoning: The upcoming earnings season for hyperscalers is the most important near-term market catalyst to watch. The critical question is whether any hyperscaler signals that AI capital expenditure may be approaching a peak, which would be highly destabilising. The base case is that AI capex continues and earnings are fine. If earnings disappoint, markets are in a precarious position given how much of the recent recovery has rotated back into hyperscalers. Semiconductor companies are also expected to report strong earnings but any commentary about double-ordering could also move markets.
quote: Is there going to be any hyperscaler that is going to suggest that their AI capex may be peaking? That would be causing quite a bit of a stir. I don't think that will happen yet. So and the earnings are likely to be fine again. So then we have nothing to worry about. And what if they're not? If they're not, markets must be in a precarious position right now. Oh, yeah, we've seen that rotation, right? So that's gone back to the hyperscalers, essentially. And some of the semiconductor companies will, I'm sure, report fantastic earnings. But there too, are they going to make some statements about double earnings or double ordering that they're seeing then that could quite lead to some impact on markets?

headline: Earnings revisions continue to rise strongly in the US and Japan, providing fundamental justification for higher equity market valuations
reasoning: Upward earnings revisions continue at a phenomenal pace, particularly in the US and Japan. This provides a fundamental basis for equity markets to trade at higher levels. The implication is that as long as this earnings momentum is sustained, higher valuations are justified, even if individual stocks are increasingly volatile and sentiment is elevated.
quote: The upward revisions we're seeing in earnings talking about that theme indeed is still phenomenal, particularly in the US and Japan. Earnings revisions keep going higher. And that means that stock markets also deserve to trade higher as long as it lasts.

headline: US banks delivering stellar earnings from IPO and M&A fees but may be reaching an 'as good as it gets' moment given share prices have already doubled
reasoning: US banks posted strong results, including significant fee income from the SpaceX IPO and broader M&A activity. Higher interest rates also provide a tailwind for net interest income. However, share prices did not respond favourably after results, suggesting the good news is already priced in. Many bank stocks have already doubled over the past 12 months. Jamie Dimon himself was sounding more cautious. AI is extending into financial services through increased bond issuance, equity issuance and IPO activity, all generating more fees, but the risk is this represents a cyclical peak.
quote: There's a bit of a as good as it gets issue here. And that indeed, you did see the share price has not respond all too favourably or sort of losing their initial jump after the results were published, which seems to suggest, OK, this is what's already in the price. But don't forget that some of these stocks have already doubled over the past 12 months, right? And to that extent, and I think Jamie Dimon was also speaking to that. AI is becoming extended into the financial sector because the capex going on there leads to so many bond issuance leads to equity issuance leads to IPO's, meaning more fees for investment bankers and banks in general. So therefore, yeah, they are also beneficiaries. And of course, then higher interest rates are a nice thing for banks too. So yeah, lots of positives there for the banks, but maybe there isn't as good as it gets moments.

headline: Micron flagged capacity shortages and spiking memory prices, blaming Apple's historical margin pressure for under-investment in capacity
reasoning: Micron's CEO publicly blamed Apple for the current spike in memory prices, arguing that Apple's persistent pressure to reduce supplier margins left Micron without the capital to invest in capacity at an earlier stage. The company is now running short of capacity just as AI-driven demand is surging. Micron was also cited as one of the names where leveraged ETFs are amplifying individual stock volatility.
quote: Micron actually mentioned in one of its analyst calls that they blame Apple for the current enormous spike that you see in memory prices, because Apple has always been very, very tight on allowing margins to these memory companies and saying, no, this must be cheaper. No, this must be cheaper. And that's why the Micron CEO said it is because of you that we did not have the money to invest at an earlier stage. And now we're running out of capacity.

headline: AI infrastructure build-out is structurally inflationary across memory, electricity, steel, transformers and cooling equipment
reasoning: The AI capex cycle is driving massive demand for a wide range of inputs including memory chips, electricity, steel, transformers and cooling equipment, all of which are seeing price pressure. Apple raising iPad prices by 20% due to surging memory costs is an early visible sign that goods prices may start to reflect these input pressures. The Micron CEO explicitly blamed Apple's historically tight margin squeeze on memory suppliers for under-investment that has now resulted in a capacity shortage. Rising electricity demand from both data centres and air conditioning compounds the inflationary dynamic.
quote: So far, we haven't really seen that in goods prices, but the move by Apple was quite interesting from that point of view that they raised iPad prices by 20 percent, saying, well, the bill of materials has gone up so dramatically for the memory that's inside these devices that we must do this. And initially, the market was a bit shocked by that. But later, it recovered and Apple has made a new all-time high, showing their wonderful pricing power. What was interesting to note there is that Micron actually mentioned in one of its analyst calls that they blame Apple for the current enormous spike that you see in memory prices, because Apple has always been very, very tight on allowing margins to these memory companies.

headline: Hyperscaler bond issuance wave is causing credit market indigestion, with spreads widening even as broader market spreads stay flat
reasoning: SpaceX's $29 billion bond issuance was well oversubscribed but the bond fell 4% in the week after issuance, rattling investment grade investors. Amazon followed with an unexpected $25 billion issuance, raising concern about the volume of paper coming to market. Hyperscaler spreads have risen while the rest of the market has been flat, signalling indigestion. Simultaneously, the underlying government bond rate (US approaching 4.6%, German bunds above 3%) is creeping higher, meaning total refinancing costs are rising sharply even if spreads remain historically low.
quote: You do see some indigestion. So for instance, the spreads of these hyperscalers have risen while the rest of the market spreads have actually been quite flat over the last couple of months. So that indigestion seems to be something that is happening in the market. But it's also a fact of the matter that the underlying base rate, i.e. the government bond rate is creeping higher as well. Right, so US bonds are creeping towards 4.6%. Now German government bonds are well above 3 again. So that base rate is also creeping up. So the total cost of refinancing for a lot of these bond issuers is creeping up quite a bit. The spreads are still low, but the total cost is actually quite high.

headline: Inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored as oil prices rebound and consumer/business surveys show elevated medium-term inflation fears
reasoning: While the latest US inflation print was moderate, the more worrying signal is that medium and longer-term inflation expectations in consumer and business surveys remain elevated. The rebound in oil prices over recent weeks reinforces fears that inflation will be a lingering problem, leaving central banks with little room to cut and some residual risk of hikes. The core concern is that if inflation expectations become unanchored, the consequences for markets and policy would be severe. There is also a perceived erosion of trust in governments and central banks to manage the problem.
quote: It's not really the issue, but the issue seems to be more that the people seem to think there is going to be more inflation. Yeah, and that's what we're seeing in various surveys of consumers and businesses. And if you look at various financial market measures, that the medium and longer term expectations on inflation is still higher. So to be clear, we know inflation in the US and Europe has been above target, the 2% target for some time. So there probably is reason to be a little concerned about the inflation outlook and central banks' ability to keep things in check. And the real issue here is that the risk is that our inflation expectations become unanchored. And that is ultimately a huge problem.

headline: Apple demonstrated strong pricing power by raising iPad prices 20% due to higher memory costs, stock recovered to all-time highs
reasoning: Apple raised iPad prices by 20%, citing a dramatic rise in the bill of materials driven by memory costs. The market was initially shocked but subsequently recovered, with Apple making a new all-time high. This is seen as evidence of Apple's exceptional pricing power. Separately, Micron's CEO attributed the spike in memory prices partly to Apple's historically aggressive margin pressure on suppliers, which discouraged earlier capacity investment and has now led to a supply shortage.
quote: The move by Apple was quite interesting from that point of view that they raised iPad prices by 20 percent, saying, well, the bill of materials has gone up so dramatically for the memory that's inside these devices that we must do this. And initially, the market was a bit shocked by that. But later, it recovered and Apple has made a new all-time high, showing their wonderful pricing power.

headline: Individual stock volatility at career-high levels driven by leveraged ETFs amplifying price moves in high-flying large-cap names including Nvidia and Micron
reasoning: While the VIX remains low, individual stock volatility for large-cap names is at the highest levels seen in careers spanning decades, according to both Adnod and Robeco's Michael Plachman. The key driver is leveraged ETFs, which require delta hedging that amplifies existing moves — buying more when stocks rise and selling when they fall. This phenomenon has become so significant in Korea that regulators have banned new leveraged ETFs. In the US, leveraged ETFs on names like Nvidia and Micron are contributing to the same dynamic.
quote: There is a bit of leverage in the system that explains this to a large extent. And one of the things that's become very topical in today's discussions, both in the US as well as now in Korea, are these leveraged ETFs, where people are saying, well, it's not enough that my SK high-neck stocks jumps 5% or 10% per day. I wanted to go double on that. And the ETF suppliers are happy to comply and offer that. And what you're seeing right now is that these are reaching levels where they do play an important role in the overall trading volume in the market, meaning that if the stock goes up, the leveraged ETFs need to buy more, right? They do the delta hedging. And if the stock goes down, then they need to reduce position. So they amplify the move that are already there.

headline: US and European central banks likely to hold rates and take a 'wait and see' approach at summer meetings as recent inflation prints remain moderate
reasoning: The latest US and European inflation data do not warrant additional concern, partly because lower oil prices through May and June helped moderate the prints. However, the recent rebound in oil prices means central banks will want to monitor the pass-through before making any move. Adnod expects an extended pause with no major policy changes at the upcoming summer monetary policy meetings.
quote: The latest European and US inflation numbers don't give rise to much more worry. And of course, that's also a translation from the reduction in oil prices that we saw through May and June. So central banks will probably take away and see attitude and see what the backup in oil prices recently will do with inflation. So they'll also take an extended summer break, I'm quite sure.

headline: El Niño confirmed and driving agri-commodity price spikes in grains, cotton, cocoa and coffee, adding to inflationary pressures
reasoning: El Niño has returned and temperatures have risen to critical trigger levels, meaning harvests will generally disappoint over the next year. Prices of grains, cotton, cocoa and coffee have already spiked in response. Combined with rising electricity demand from data centres and increased air conditioning usage driven by heatwaves, these forces are collectively feeding through into broader inflationary pressure. The European continent is heating up particularly fast, running two to three degrees above historical base levels.
quote: The main phenomenon is that El Nino is back, and that's causing agri-comology prices to spike over the last couple of weeks, as it's been confirmed that indeed those temperatures have risen to the critical levels to trigger an El Nino. And that means that the harvests will generally be less than expected for the next year. So you saw some of the grains go up quite a bit. Cotton was up, cocoa was up, and even coffee was up. So heatwaves and all the other stuff, yeah, it's all leading to more inflation.

headline: EM tech stocks offer AI-linked growth at materially cheaper valuations than developed market peers, making them an attractive alternative to DM tech
reasoning: Kostich highlights that investors can now access technology stocks in emerging markets that offer high growth expectations and AI exposure at significantly lower valuations than their developed market equivalents. This makes EM tech a compelling alternative to DM technology. Client flows into Robeco's EM quant strategies have been strong on the back of this dynamic combined with broader EM outperformance.
quote: We see very attractive valuations, the opportunities are there, the growth expectations are really high. And now you can get also exposure to tech stocks that are offering this growth, but at much cheaper valuations that you would have in developed markets. So it's a very attractive alternative than just to go to DM.
episode_title: Emerging markets, concentration risk and the evolution of quantitative investing

headline: Emerging market index has become heavily concentrated in tech, with technology now over 40% and three names representing over 30% of the index
reasoning: Moselar acknowledges that EM indices have become increasingly skewed toward tech stocks, mirroring the Magnificent Seven concentration in the S&P 500. Technology now accounts for more than 40% of the EM index, with just three names constituting more than 30%. However, he notes that not all tech stocks behave identically as they occupy different parts of the AI and tech value chain. Robeco's broad 3,000-stock universe allows it to diversify beyond these heavily weighted index names.
quote: In DM, this has been the case for many years already with magnificent seven dominating the S&P 500. But also in EM, there's no denial that the emerging market index has become very skewed towards tech stocks. If you look at the technology sector, it's now more than 40% of the index. Three names are more than 30% of the index. So yeah, you could say it's become crowded, it's become more concentrated. There is some truth in that. At the same time, not all tech stocks behave in the same way. They all have their different place in the AI or tech value chain.
episode_title: Emerging markets, concentration risk and the evolution of quantitative investing

headline: Robeco quant sees emerging markets at the outset of a long period of outperformance versus developed markets
reasoning: Moselar notes a significant valuation gap between emerging markets and developed markets, with EM stocks still attractively valued even in the technology space despite a recent bull run. He highlights that earnings growth, which had been lacking for a decade, has returned in full force driven by the tech boom alongside healthy fundamentals. He would not be surprised if this marks the start of a long-term period of EM outperformance versus other parts of the world. He is personally invested heavily in emerging markets for this reason.
quote: When you look at the valuation, there's still quite a big valuation gap. Also, when you look long-term, you have these big waves of DM versus EM outperformance. I think we're at the, well, we could be at the outset of a long period of emerging markets outperformance. So what we look at with our quant models, we do see that a lot of emerging market stocks are quite attractive value still, even in the technology space. So yeah, we do find still a lot of stocks that are very attractive, despite the recent bull market, because you could get fear of heights in these environments. But if you look longer term, the emerging markets are still very attractively valued versus other parts of the world.
episode_title: Emerging markets, concentration risk and the evolution of quantitative investing

headline: Robeco quant model moved from overweight to underweight Chinese platform names as earnings revisions turned negative amid e-commerce price war
reasoning: Approximately one to two years ago, Robeco held an overweight in large Chinese platform internet names as momentum, earnings revisions and quality metrics were all positive. However, a price war broke out in the Chinese e-commerce ecosystem, compressing profitability across these companies. As earnings revisions and momentum turned negative, the model reduced the position to an underweight. Robeco has thus been less impacted by the ongoing negative earnings adjustments affecting these names.
quote: Two years, one and a half years ago, the Chinese platform names were really popular. So, well, the big names in the Chinese platform internet ecosystem. These names went up a lot. And we basically, we had an overweight. Momentum was positive, earnings revisions was positive, quality was quite good. And we had an overweight, we profited from this rise up. At a certain point, what happened in the e-commerce platform ecosystem in China was basically a price war. So basically, companies started to compete with each other. That's good for the consumer because they got lower prices, but it's bad for the profitability of these companies. And what we saw is that the earnings provisions turned negative, momentum turned negatively. And basically, the whole sentiment around these stocks changed, and also the earnings were impacted. So also the fundamentals changed. This was picked up by our model. We went from overweight to an underweight.
episode_title: Emerging markets, concentration risk and the evolution of quantitative investing

headline: Robeco quant model currently holds slight overweight in Korean tech and broadly balanced exposure across Asian hardware ecosystem
reasoning: Moselar explains that Robeco's most active EM strategy currently has a slight overweight in Korean tech companies and a modest underweight in some Taiwanese tech companies, though overall exposure to the Asian hardware ecosystem is fairly balanced. Bottom-up stock selection within the sector has been successful. The broad universe of 3,000 EM stocks allows the model to find attractive Asian hardware names beyond the three mega-cap index names.
quote: If you currently look for our most active EM strategy, we have a slight overweight in Korean tech companies and some underweight in some of the Taiwanese tech companies. But overall, it's quite balanced. So if you look at the overall Asian hardware ecosystem, we have quite a balanced exposure to that. But the stock selection within that has been pretty successful.
episode_title: Emerging markets, concentration risk and the evolution of quantitative investing

headline: Korean market cross-holdings create structural pricing discounts that Robeco's quant model can exploit as an alpha source
reasoning: Moselar highlights that the Korean market is notorious for complex cross-holdings structures that generate discounts between related securities. Similarly, differences between preferred and ordinary shares, US-listed ADRs versus local shares, and Chinese A-shares versus Hong Kong H-shares create exploitable pricing imbalances. Robeco's quant approach is able to select the more attractively priced listing while maintaining the same underlying economic exposure.
quote: We can profit from imbalances, for example, cross holdings for a Korean market is notorious for that. So you have all these different cross holdings that create discounts, for example, we can profit from that. So the model is typically blind for these things, preferred shares versus ordinary shares, or us listed ADRs versus local shares.
